payload.name: Activity Duration Queries Include Event Memories
payload.description: When a question asks how long a recurring or typical activity takes (e.g., 'how long does X walk/run/do Y?'), search event memories and use duration-specific phrasing.
content: When a question asks how long a habitual activity takes (e.g., 'how long does Audrey typically walk her dogs?'), do not restrict the search to profile or state memories; include the event memory kind because routine activity durations are commonly stored as event facts.
Add query variants that include 'usually lasts', 'typically', 'about', and 'duration of [activity]' alongside the activity keywords.
If an event memory directly states the duration, stop searching and answer with that duration; do not substitute a related event date or unrelated activity.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask how long a habitual activity takes (e.g., how long someone typically walks their dog) fail when retrieval is restricted to profile/state memories, because routine activity durations are often stored in event memories. This skill adds event-memory search and duration-specific query variants so the answering agent can find the direct duration fact.

payload.name: Date-filtered search without date literal
payload.description: When a question asks what someone did on a specific date and the first date-filtered search includes the date literal, rerun the search with the time filter but without the date text in the query.
content: When a question targets an event on a specific calendar date, do not put the date literal (e.g., 'December 4, 2023') into the query text or keywords if you are already applying a time filter; the memory may express the date relatively (e.g., 'yesterday', 'last Monday') and will fail to match the literal date string.

If the initial structured search uses the date literal and returns no memory with world_start on that date, rerun the search with memory_kind 'event', time_mode 'point' and target_time set to the date, but use only the person's name plus an event-related term (e.g., 'attended', 'went to', 'meeting', 'activity') as the query; check for memories whose world_start equals the target date even if their text lacks the date string.
Stop after this one additional search; if it still returns no relevant memory, answer with no information and do not broaden to other dates.

candidates.solves: Fixes date-specific event questions that fail because the query includes the date literal while the stored memory uses a relative time expression (e.g., 'yesterday') that resolves to the target date, causing the memory to be missed by retrieval.

payload.name: Include Plan Memories for Planned Event Questions
payload.description: When a question asks when or whether a person is planning a future event (e.g., reunion, trip, gathering, project), include memory_kind 'plan' in searches instead of restricting to events only.
content: If the question asks about a planned future event (planning, plans, intends, wants to organize, is going to), run structured or hybrid searches with memory_kind including 'plan' as well as 'event'; do not restrict memory_kinds to event when the question is about a plan.
Use relative time words in the question (next summer, next week, soon) to evaluate the plan's world_start or its described timing after retrieving plan memories.
If the first searches return only event memories and no plan memory, run one additional search filtered to memory_kind=plan with the same query before answering; stop after that retry.

candidates.solves: Questions about planned future events are often answered from plan memories, but retrieval frequently filters to event memories and misses the plan. This skill ensures plan-kind memories are included and relative time phrases are used when the question asks about a plan.

payload.name: List Answers Enumerate All Stated Items
payload.description: When a question asks for a list of items a person made, read, watched, or otherwise did, use this to ensure every distinct item explicitly named in retrieved evidence is included in the answer.
content: For list-type questions such as 'What [items] has [person] [made/read/watched]?', after retrieval identify every distinct named item for which the subject is directly stated as performing the action.
Enumerate each named item separately, even if it appears in only one memory or is subsumed by a broader term; use the most specific name available.
If the same item appears in multiple memories with slight wording differences, report it once using the most complete name.
Stop after checking all retrieved memories; do not infer or add items not explicitly stated as performed by the subject.

candidates.solves: When answering list questions about things a person has made or done, the agent often omits directly supported items from retrieved evidence, leading to incomplete answers. This skill ensures the agent enumerates every distinct item explicitly named in the retrieved memories, rather than dropping some while adding loosely related alternatives.

payload.name: Directional claim verification for multi-person questions
payload.description: When a question names two people and a directional action (A watched/recommended/suggested X to B) and the top result reverses the direction or covers only one person, verify before answering.
content: When a question names two people and a directional action (A watched/recommended/suggested/gave X to B), a retrieved memory that reverses the direction or involves only one person is insufficient; do not answer from it.

Run a follow-up search for each named person using their name plus action terms (e.g., watched, recommended, suggested, gave) without requiring the question's date, since the supporting memory may be dated differently.

Before answering, verify the candidate memory supports the claimed actor, action, and recipient; if not, keep searching until one memory covers all claims or separate per-person searches have been exhausted.
Stop as soon as a memory covers all claims in the question; do not retrieve additional unrelated events.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask what one person watched, recommended, suggested, or gave to another on a specific date are sometimes answered from a partial or direction-reversed memory that merely shares a date or keyword. This skill ensures the agent verifies actor-action-recipient alignment and runs per-person follow-up searches before committing to an answer.

payload.name: Answer with All Enumerated Supported Causes
payload.description: When a question asks what cause(s) or issue(s) a person supports, advocates for, or uses influence and resources for, and the retrieved evidence lists multiple enumerated aspects, include every listed aspect in the answer.
content: When the user asks what cause, issue, or area a person supports or advocates for, examine the supporting memory for all explicitly enumerated aspects (e.g., a compound phrase like 'supporting X and fighting for Y').
If the evidence contains two or more such aspects, answer with all of them as a combined answer; do not stop at the first aspect merely because the question contains 'one cause'.
Only report causes explicitly present in retrieved evidence; do not add additional causes from general knowledge or inference.

candidates.solves: Answering questions about a person's supported causes or issues often omits the second of two explicitly enumerated aspects from the same retrieved memory, producing an incomplete answer despite sufficient evidence.

payload.name: Enumerate all techniques for multi-person queries
payload.description: When a question asks what methods, techniques, strategies, or tools one or more people use, and the initial search returns only partial evidence, apply this before answering.
content: Parse the question for named people and the topic (e.g., time management, studying, organization); determine whether the question seeks a list (plural 'techniques', 'methods', 'tools', 'strategies').

After an initial hybrid search with the topic and all named people, run separate hybrid searches for each named person combining their name, the topic, and common technique synonyms (e.g., 'Pomodoro', 'to-do list', 'schedule', 'planner', 'matrix', 'journal', 'app', 'calendar').
Do not require a technique memory to contain the person's name; consider memories that mention the technique name alone when the person is identified from context or other memories.
Stop after two additional searches per person, or as soon as a search returns no new distinct technique; answer only from visible evidence.

candidates.solves: A question asking what methods, techniques, strategies, or tools one or more people use (e.g., time management techniques) can be answered incompletely if the agent performs a single generic search and misses memories that name specific techniques. The agent needs a rule to expand the search per person and with technique-name synonyms, then stop after bounded attempts.

payload.name: Search major life domains for hardship causes
payload.description: When a question asks why someone has been going through a tough time, struggling, or facing challenges, include searches for major life domains (employment, health, relationships, finances) before concluding.
content: When a question asks why a person has been having a tough time, struggling, or facing recent difficulties, do not stop after generic searches for 'stress' or 'challenges'.
Run at least one additional search per major life domain: employment/career (e.g., 'job', 'work', 'laid off', 'fired'), health, and relationships, using the person's name with each domain keyword.

If an event memory describing a recent major change or loss in any of these domains is found, consider it the likely cause and answer from that evidence; only answer with minor stressors if no major life event is found.

candidates.solves: Generic searches for 'stress' or 'difficulties' often miss event memories about major life changes like job loss, which are the actual cause of a person's recent hardship. This skill ensures retrieval covers employment, health, relationships, and finances.

payload.name: Search Superlative Performance Memories
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a person's career-high, best, highest, record, or top performance, especially within a specified time period. Apply before answering.
content: When a question asks about career-high/best/record performances, do not search only with the literal phrase 'career-high'; add paraphrases like 'highest ever', 'best', 'personal best', 'record', and 'top' combined with the person's name and the relevant stat/domain (e.g., points, assists, score).

If the first results contain only one superlative performance, run at least one additional search for other stat categories or aspects before answering, because such questions often expect more than one career-high.

Treat memories with superlative language (e.g., 'highest ever score', 'career-high in X') as matching, answer only from visible evidence, and stop after each expected aspect is supported or after 3 diverse search attempts.

candidates.solves: When a question asks about a person's career-high, best, or record performances, retrieval often anchors on the literal phrase 'career-high' and stops after the first matching memory. This misses other superlative achievements stored with phrasings like 'highest ever', 'personal best', or 'record', and can omit multiple stat categories expected by the question.

payload.name: Writing Type Retrieval
payload.description: Use when a question asks what kind of writing a person does or what types of writing they engage in.
content: When asked what kind of writing someone does, do not limit retrieval to memories that explicitly say 'writing' or to formal works (articles, books, scripts).
Run additional searches using the person's name combined with informal writing contexts: 'forum', 'discussion', 'comments', 'reviews', 'recommendations', 'posts', 'blogs'.
Include memory kinds event, preference, and profile; the activity may be recorded as participation in a discussion or a recommendation rather than as an explicit writing event.
Merge results across searches and stop once distinct writing types are clear or after two or three search attempts without new types.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask what kind of writing a person does often return only formal writing memories (articles, books) and miss informal writing venues such as forum comments, discussion posts, reviews, or recommendations. This skill guides retrieval to include those informal contexts so the answer reflects all writing-related activities.

payload.name: Creative Output Versus Consumption Preference
payload.description: When asked what kind of fiction, stories, or creative works a person writes or creates, do not infer from what they read/watch; retrieve their creation activity memories instead.
content: When asked what kind of fiction/stories/works a person writes, search with creation verbs and nouns: writes, writing, novel, story, create, working on, project, draft, plot, genre; do not answer from reading/watching preference memories alone.
Include memory kinds event, plan, and state; current writing projects are often stored as in-progress events or plans, not as preferences.
After finding a creation memory, run one follow-up search for story elements (plot, twist, character, theme) linked to that work before answering.
Stop once the genre and explicitly stated story elements are found; do not expand to unrelated works.

candidates.solves: Questions about what kind of stories or creative works a person writes are often answered from their reading/watching preferences, which may differ from what they actually create. Direct evidence about writing projects in event/plan/state memories is missed, along with associated story features like plot twists. This skill ensures retrieval targets creation activity and follows up on story details.

payload.name: Retrieve skills a person helped others learn
payload.description: When a question asks what skills, recipes, or abilities someone taught or helped others learn, use before answering.
content: Run multiple targeted searches with varied phrasings: 'taught', 'helped', 'shared', 'showed', 'tips', 'assisted', 'learned from'.

Do not restrict retrieval to event memories; include profile, state, relationship, and preference memories because teaching/helping may be encoded indirectly as sharing creations or supporting others.

After the first supporting memory, check whether the question implies multiple distinct skills; if so, keep searching for additional distinct skills until each is either supported or a supplementary search finds no new candidate.
Stop after two supplementary searches yield no new distinct skill; do not expand exhaustively.

candidates.solves: When an access agent must answer questions that enumerate the skills or abilities a person has helped others learn, it often stops after one supporting memory or searches only with literal 'taught/learn' phrasing. This misses indirectly stored teaching/helping evidence such as sharing creations, offering tips, or helping with a task. The skill guides broader synonym searches across memory kinds and continued checking until each distinct skill is either supported or ruled out.

payload.name: Possession origin retrieval across memory kinds
payload.description: When a question asks how someone got, obtained, acquired, or adopted a possession or pet, use this before answering 'No information available'.
content: For 'how did X get/obtain/adopt Y' questions, do not restrict the first search to event memories; include relationship, profile, and state memory kinds because the acquisition source or method is often stored as a fact (e.g., 'Luna was adopted from a shelter').

If the first event-only search returns no acquisition memory, run one more search with the same person and item but without a memory_kinds filter, or explicitly include 'relationship' and 'profile' kinds, before concluding no information is available.
Stop after one additional non-event search returns no new acquisition evidence; do not expand exhaustively.

candidates.solves: This solves cases where a question asks how a person acquired a possession or pet, but the acquisition method is stored in a relationship, profile, or state memory rather than an event memory; the agent currently restricts to event memories and misses the answer.

payload.name: Count owned items across event and profile memories
payload.description: When a question asks how many of a category a person has or owns and no direct summary count exists, search event plus profile/state memories, not just acquisition events.
content: When counting items a person owns or possesses, do not limit retrieval to event memories. Also run structured or hybrid searches across profile, state, and event memory kinds using the entity plus the category (e.g., "<name>'s dogs", "<name> owns", "<name> has a pet") and predicates like owns, has, pet.

Enumerate distinct named instances from both acquisition events and profile/state ownership facts; count those whose world_start is on or before the target date and whose world_end, if any, is after the target date.
When an event or plan mentions a named companion, inspect or search profile/state memories for that name to confirm whether ownership already exists before counting or excluding it.
Stop after retrieving all candidate instances or after one additional targeted search that returns no new instances; do not exhaustively expand.

candidates.solves: Answers undercount or overcount ownership/possession questions because retrieval is restricted to acquisition event memories, while current possessions are often stored as profile or state facts and acquisition events may not match the chosen keywords.

payload.name: Search Family and Friends for Loss Queries with Indirect Evidence
payload.description: When a question asks which of a named person's family and friends have died or passed away, search each known relation and friend using death and grief terms, and accept indirect memorial language as evidence.
content: When a question asks who among a named person's family and friends has died/passed away, treat it as a multi-entity loss query: run targeted searches for each family relation (mother, father, spouse, siblings, etc.) and each named friend that appears in the session or retrieved memories, combined with death terms (passed away, died, lost).
Also search for the named person's friends generally (e.g., '<name> friend passed away', '<name> friend died') because the friend may be named only in a memory that uses indirect language.

Treat indirect grief/memorial language (finds comfort in memories of, reflects on their time together, lost a friend, in memory of) as evidence the person has died, and include such memories in the answer.
Stop after all known family and friend relations have been searched or a matching memory is found for each; do not exhaustively expand beyond the session's known relations.

candidates.solves: Answers that ask which of a person's family or friends have died often miss friends because the initial search focuses on family and explicit death words. This skill ensures friends are searched and indirect grief/memory language is recognized as evidence of death.

payload.name: Infer social connections from activities and memberships
payload.description: When a question asks whether a person has friends or companions besides a named individual, search activities, teams, and group memberships before concluding no.
content: When a question asks whether a subject has friends or social connections besides a named person, do not treat the absence of explicit 'friend' memories mentioning other people as proof of no friends.

After any initial retrieval focused on the named person, run one additional hybrid and one structured search using the subject's name with keywords for activities and group contexts (e.g., team, club, tournament, group, class, teammate, member, participated, won) and memory_kinds=['event','relationship','profile','state'].

If a retrieved memory shows the subject participating in a team, tournament, class, club, or recurring group activity, answer that it is likely they have friends or companions from that context, citing that memory.
Stop after one additional targeted search that returns no such activity or membership memories; avoid exhaustive expansion.

candidates.solves: When a question asks whether a person likely has friends or companions beyond a named individual, the agent searches only for explicit friend relationships involving that named person, missing evidence of social connections implied by activities, teams, clubs, or group events. This skill directs a targeted search for activity and membership contexts before concluding no friends exist.

payload.name: Hobby Retrieval Across Memory Kinds and Indirect References
payload.description: Use when a question asks about a named person's hobbies or interests, especially when the person is deceased, absent, or referenced through another person's memories, to ensure profile/state memories and indirect connection evidence are searched.
content: When a question asks about a named person's hobbies or interests, include memory kinds profile and state in addition to event and preference; hobbies are often stored as profile interests or state emotions/connections, not only as activities.

If the person is deceased, absent, or only referenced through another person's memories, also search indirect phrasings such as 'reminded me of <person>', 'connection through <activity>', and '<person> <activity>' from the other person's perspective, and consider explicit connection memories as candidate evidence.

Treat indirect connection/remembrance memories as evidence of the target person's hobby only when the memory explicitly links the target to the activity; if only the other person's activity is mentioned, do not infer the target's hobby without a direct or corroborating memory.
Stop once direct and indirect searches return no new distinct activities; do not keep expanding with more phrasings.

candidates.solves: When a question asks for a person's hobbies or interests, retrieval often misses evidence stored outside activity/event memories, such as profile interests or state emotions, and overlooks indirect references where the hobby appears through another person's connection (e.g., a late family member). This skill broadens memory-kind coverage and indirect-phrase searching so hobby lists are complete without exhaustive expansion.

payload.name: Count Owned Instances with Profile Search and Named Follow-up
payload.description: When counting how many of a category an entity owns as of a date and an event-only search returns plans or vague references, search profile/state memories and follow up on any named instances.
content: When counting owned items as of a target date, do not restrict to memory_kinds=['event']; also include 'profile' and 'state' because current ownership is often stored as a profile fact (e.g., 'Andrew has a dog named Toby').

If a returned memory mentions a named instance (e.g., a pet's name) or a plan involving one, run a targeted search for that name with the owner (e.g., '<owner> adopted <name>' or '<owner> <name> pet') across both event and profile memory kinds to confirm whether the acquired instance exists as of the target date.
Stop after each distinct instance is confirmed via an event or profile memory, or after one targeted search per mentioned name yields no new evidence.

candidates.solves: Counting owned items (e.g., pets) as of a target date fails when ownership is stored as a profile or state memory rather than an event, or when named instances appear only in plans or other memories and are not followed up with targeted searches, causing the agent to miss instances or count intentions as possessions.

payload.name: Search Relationship and Naming Events for Group Members
payload.description: When a question asks for the names of a person's pets, family, or group members and the first search returns activity memories without names, include relationship memories and search naming/acquisition events.
content: When a question asks for the names or identities of a person's pets, family, or group members, include relationship memory kinds (pet, family, member_of) in the search, not only event and state.

If the first search returns activity memories without names, run targeted searches for acquisition or definition events such as adopted, bought, received, named, or welcomed, combined with the person and the entity type.
Answer only from retrieved evidence; if only some names are supported, report those with their supporting memories and do not infer missing names from group size.
Stop after one relationship-kind pass and one acquisition-event pass; avoid searching indefinitely for every possible name.

candidates.solves: Questions that ask for the names of a person's pets, family members, or group members often miss evidence because generic activity-based searches return no names and relationship memory kinds are excluded from retrieval.

payload.name: Search relationship memories for owned-entity attributes
payload.description: When a question asks how old a person's pet, animal, or owned item is, include relationship memories in the search; ages and attributes are often stored in the ownership relationship memory, not only in profile/state memories.
content: When asked for the age(s) of someone's pet(s), animal(s), or owned item(s), do not restrict retrieval to profile/state memories; include relationship memories because ownership records often contain the entity's age or other attributes.

If the first search returns no direct age, run one additional targeted search using the owner's name plus the entity names and age terms (e.g., 'old', 'years old', 'age') with memory_kinds including relationship; inspect any ownership memory that names the entities.
Stop once a memory directly states the age(s); answer with the stated ages and cite the memory. Do not derive ages from unrelated events or make estimates unless no direct evidence exists.

candidates.solves: Age and attribute questions about a person's pets or owned items often fail because the target values are stored inside relationship memories (e.g., an ownership record that also states the pet's age), while the agent searches only profile/state memories and stops. This Skill ensures relationship memories are included for such attribute-of-owned-entity queries and provides a focused follow-up search before giving up.
